reading.body:
Elizabeth Frazee is named on 76 AI lobbying filings, all filed through one firm, and her disclosed clients are a mix of trade associations, telecoms, and technology companies.

The client list is the useful part. SIIA, i2Coalition, LinkedIn, X Corp., T-Mobile, and SAIC each appear on between 10 and 14 AI filings. That spread matters for AI because the policy questions these filers care about, from data and platform rules to federal procurement and national security work, are the same ones that determine where compute can be built and who can buy it. A single lobbyist carrying both a trade association and the companies it represents is a common Washington arrangement, and the filings show it here without saying anything about influence.

The prior government positions are disclosed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, which requires filers to list covered positions held in the prior twenty years. The same set of roles recurs across the filings: counsel and legislative director for Rep. Bob Goodlatte, communications director for Rep. Tom Bliley, and press secretary for the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. That committee has jurisdiction over energy and commerce matters, which is where grid and data center policy sits.

What the data does not cover is outcome. It records who was named on which filing, not what was asked for, what was spent, or what any agency did. It also does not establish that the AI filings concerned data centers or power, only that they were about AI.
